Dancing Squares

GeometryAreaInvariants
Game: A grid of stiff squares is hinged at its corners, and the squares stay the same size as the pattern opens and shuts.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Change the layers and colours, then press Open hinge to watch the pattern move.
Colour
Look for the math

Paul Brown's applet shows something unusual: a pattern of rigid squares can open out and close up again without any square changing shape or size. The live cut-the-knot page embeds the applet twice, once with the hinges locked and once with them loose. That is why this page has a Lock hinges switch. The logic test checks the page's motion claim at every angle from 1 to 179 degrees rather than taking it on trust.

Four squares on a hinge

Drag A, B or C. The fourth corner of the hinge rhombus is D = A + C − B. The applet puts one square on each side of ABCD by turning the side through a quarter turn; reflecting those four squares across their free edges grows the whole tessellation. A quarter turn keeps the two new edges at right angles and exactly as long as the side they came from, so every tile stays a square. With Lock hinges on, all four squares have the same side; switch it off and the two hinge sides can differ, so two square sizes appear.

The cell that grows

Take the length of one square's side to be s and let θ be the angle at hinge B. Two squares lie in each repeating block, and the steps between neighbouring blocks are always equal and at right angles. The test verifies, for every angle, that the block's area is

cell = 2s²(1 + sin θ), so the covered fraction is 1 / (1 + sin θ).

At θ = 0° the cell is 2s² and the squares cover it completely: a plain grid. At 90° the cell has grown to 4s² and the squares cover only half of it, sitting at opposite half-cell offsets: a checkerboard. At 180° the cell is back to 2s² and the grid is whole again. The cell grows from 0° to 90° and shrinks from 90° to 180° at every step of the test, so the page's "expand, checkerboard, reform" description is exactly right — not just a rough impression.

Why the last grid is turned

The test also measures the direction of a square's edge. It turns by half the hinge angle, from 0° at the start to 90° at the end. That is the page's claim that the grid reforms with every square rotated a quarter turn. You can reach that final grid by opening the hinges clockwise or counterclockwise, which is why some squares end up turned one way and some the other. The quantity that never changes along either route is the side length s: the rigid-square invariant.

What the applet leaves out

The Java applet's information string still says "Pythagorean Theorem, Proof #36", which is a leftover from a different applet; nothing in this pattern uses that proof, so this page follows the cut-the-knot article instead. The second layer-growing routine in the bytecode is also never called by Compute(), so it changes nothing you can see. The test transcribes the called routines a second time and checks all sixteen layers for scores of starting shapes.

Press Reset, then Open hinge nine times: the hinge reaches 90° and the status line announces a checkerboard. Close it nine times to get back to the plain grid.
